content: The following information provides a detailed overview of Panax ginseng (Asian ginseng) and its clinical considerations, including dosing, potential adverse effects, interactions, contraindications, and use during pregnancy and lactation: Dosing Recommendations: Oral Dosing: 6–3 grams taken once daily to three times daily (qDay–TID). 3 grams taken orally once daily to three times daily (qDay–TID). 900 mg taken orally three times daily (TID). 200 mg taken orally once daily (qDay). 100–300 mg of standardized extract (containing 7% ginsenosides) taken three times daily (TID) for 3–4 weeks. Topical Use: Cream applied one hour prior to intercourse and washed off before intercourse. Indications and Effects: Adaptogen: Helps the body adapt to internal and external stressors, combats fatigue, and enhances stamina. Potential Uses: Anxiety, athletic/physical stamina enhancement, cognitive function improvement, depression, male fertility, headaches, immune stimulation, menopausal hot flashes, and impotence. Efficacy: Possibly Effective: Cognitive function, diabetes, erectile dysfunction, and premature ejaculation. Possibly Ineffective: Athletic performance, menopausal symptoms, and quality of life. Insufficient Evidence: Breast cancer, bronchitis, cancer, common cold, congestive heart failure, and influenza. Adverse Effects: Commonly reported side effects include: Allergic skin reactions, amenorrhea, decreased appetite, cerebral arteritis, cholestatic hepatitis, diarrhea, edema, euphoria, headache, hyperpyrexia, hypertension, hypotension, insomnia, mania, mastalgia, neonatal death, palpitations, pruritus, rose spots, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, tachycardia, vaginal bleeding, and vertigo. Contraindications: Panax ginseng should be avoided in individuals with: Bleeding disorders, breast cancer, endometrial cancer, endometriosis, estrogen-dependent malignancies, diabetes, hormone-sensitive conditions, hypertension, hypersensitivity, neonates, organ transplant recipients, ovarian cancer, pregnancy, thromboembolic disorders, and uterine fibroids. Drug and Herb Interactions: Anticoagulation Risk: Panax ginseng increases anticoagulant effects when combined with numerous drugs and herbs, including aspirin, heparin, warfarin, NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac), and natural products like garlic, ginger, ginkgo biloba, and cinnamon. Close monitoring or therapy modification is recommended in these cases. Pharmacodynamic Synergism: Panax ginseng may enhance the effects of antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline, fluoxetine, sertraline), insulin (e.g., insulin aspart, insulin glargine), and other medications through pharmacodynamic interactions. The clinical significance of these interactions is often unknown but warrants caution. Unclear Interactions: Panax ginseng may interact with mistletoe, nettle, and vitamin K1, with unclear effects on anticoagulation. Caution is advised. Pregnancy and Lactation: Pregnancy: Classified as Category X, indicating that it is contraindicated during pregnancy due to evidence of fetal risk. Lactation: No available data to support its safety during breastfeeding. Special Considerations: Use caution in patients with cardiovascular disease, concurrent use of CYP2D6 substrates, diabetes mellitus, insomnia, schizophrenia, or in pediatric populations. This information highlights the importance of careful consideration when using Panax ginseng, particularly in patients with pre-existing conditions or those taking medications with potential interactions. Always consult a healthcare provider before initiating therapy.
